claims.text: For a C# class (reference type) that is not a record, == compares references unless the type overloads the == operator; a class that defines no equality of its own gets reference equality from == and Equals.
claims.source_hint: C# language reference: Equality operators (reference types equality); Equality comparisons (C# Programming Guide)

claims.text: Stage-2 Order defines no equality of its own: no == operator, no Equals or GetHashCode override, and it is a class, not a record.
Two separate HTTP requests each get their own scoped DonHangDbContext, so loading order 6 in each produces two distinct Order instances.
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: DbContext lifetime, configuration and initialization (AddDbContext registers a scoped context, one per request)

claims.text: Code asking whether two orders are the same order should compare their Id values, not references and not all fields; DDD entities are equal by identity.
Customer, Product and Order each declare public int Id { get; set; }; OrderItem has no Id property, only OrderId, ProductId, Quantity and UnitPriceVnd.
EF Core calls each class in its model an entity type (Customer, Order and OrderItem included), usually mapped to a table; OrderItem's key is composite (OrderId, ProductId).
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Creating and configuring a model > Entity types; Keys (composite keys); DonHangDbContext.cs:68-71 @ stage-2

claims.text: EF Core needs a key on an entity type to track it and insert or update its row; keyless entity types (HasNoKey) exist but are never tracked or updated. EF Core does not model whether the business follows the row over time.
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Keys ('a key serves as a unique identifier for each entity instance'); Keyless entity types (never tracked for changes)

claims.text: PlaceOrderAsync (OrderService) receives the request's Idempotency-Key header value (OrdersController [FromHeader]) and recognises a retry by it (FindByIdempotencyKeyAsync), not by comparing items; each new order gets its own Id and notification.
Whether a class is a DDD entity depends on whether the business follows each instance over time; having an Id property or an EF Core mapping does not decide it.
At stage-2 staff can change a product's price (PATCH in ProductsController under the StaffOnly policy), and the product keeps its Id.
